L'accompagnement juridique des personnes: Legal support for migrants with precarious status or no status: a lottery they often lose
« Aujourd’hui, être un migrant et avoir: “Today, being a migrant with temporary status or no status means having enormous difficulty accessing the law”
Louis-Philippe Jannard, coordonnateur du: Louis-Philippe Jannard, coordinator of the protection component at the Table de concertation des organismes au service des personnes réfugiées et immigrantes (TCRI). Photo credit: Ismaël Koné
<strong>Insécurité, incertitudes, angois: Insecurity, uncertainty, anxiety: this is the daily lot of many temporary immigrants in Canada. Many have precarious status or no status, very often through no choice of their own. Legal support is crucial for finding a way through the administrative maze that can lead to permanent status, but access to good legal representation is complicated. On World Refugee Day, we take a closer look at this problem. Report.
« Après avoir obtenu mes papiers, j’ai s: “After I got my papers, I suffered a very serious depression that forced me to take medication,” Maria*, who arrived in Montréal 15 years ago, fleeing threats from a cartel, tells us. “The shock of not seeing my family for so long, of leaving my culture, of wondering whether everything I had been through was worth it (...) Wow, there were so many complicated things! And all of that because a lawyer didn’t do his job.”
Maria se remet à peine d’une longue trav: Maria is barely recovering from a long trek through the wilderness: 10 years of bureaucratic wandering in Canada and the constant burden of being poorly represented by a whole series of immigration lawyers, from either legal aid or the private sector. Those lawyers nonetheless cost her nearly $7,000, an astronomical sum given her financial precarity.
Formulaire de demande d’asile mal rempli: An asylum claim form filled out incorrectly, a lost file, a lack of commitment, even outright carelessness in defending her case: Maria had to deal with several situations in which her lawyers let her down. In her living room, she tells us about her misadventures, her six years without papers and the sleepless nights all of it caused her.
« J’ai pris la décision de payer mon pro: “I made the decision to pay for my own lawyer, who in 2012 was charging me $200 an hour. Even if it was just for two questions, a 10-minute interview, I had to pay that amount,” she explains.
Elle se souvient des imbroglios administ: She remembers the administrative tangles: “There was a very long string of lawyers. The first one had made a mistake. It had a domino effect that carried on over time, (…) You had to fix the previous lawyer’s mistake, and in the meantime, the errors piled up.”
« Un avocat est plus qu’un représentant: “A lawyer is more than a legal representative. Literally, he holds your life in his hands. Your future depends on him.”
Sa situation s’arrange enfin lorsqu’elle: Her situation finally improves when she meets <l1>Solidarity Across Borders</l1>, a Montréal-based network of immigrant struggles. “I got involved with the Centre des travailleurs migrants, where I received support from different people in various areas,” says Maria.
Ces difficultés d’accès à un service jur: These difficulties in accessing quality legal services faced by migrants with precarious status and no status in Quebec were the subject of <l1>a study published by a group of researchers</l1> in early June. It is an initiative of the Solutions justes legal clinic of the Mission communautaire de Montréal.
« Aujourd’hui, être un migrant et avoir: “Today, being a migrant with temporary status or no status means having enormous difficulty accessing the law,” explains Delphine Nakache, full professor at the Faculty of Law of the University of Ottawa and holder of the University Research Chair on the Protection of Migrants and International Law. “Why? Because the system is poorly funded and because the needs of migrants with precarious status aren’t recognized: their need for protection, their need for regularization, their needs in other areas of the law.”
Les personnes migrantes en situation pré: Migrants in precarious situations or without status form a very diverse group, characterized by the absence of permanent residence or work authorization and by dependence on a third party for housing or employment. They also have difficulty accessing public services and the protection system, including health care and education, and they risk deportation. In Canada, this status applies both to people in a regular but temporary situation (foreign workers, students, asylum seekers awaiting a decision) and to people whose administrative situation is unstable (expired visa, rejected asylum claim).
Groupe de chercheuses ayant mené l'étude: The group of researchers who carried out the study on the difficulties in accessing quality legal services faced by migrants with precarious status and no status in Quebec. Photo credit: Ismaël Koné
Selon les chercheuses, la majeure partie: According to the researchers, most people enter the country with legal status, and a number of them then lose that status for reasons that are often beyond their control.
« Ça peut être une perte d’emploi, un em: “It can be a job loss, an abusive employer, a case of domestic violence, or some other trigger that leads the person, at some point, to end up in a precarious situation. So what you have to understand is that today, there is a lot of luck in the immigration system,” says Delphine Nakache.
Olga Houde a travaillé pendant huit ans: Olga Houde worked for eight years at the <l1>Solutions Justes clinic</l1>, a program aimed at improving access to justice for immigrants and refugees. Many of the people supported there have had negative experiences with legal support, but 99 per cent of the people followed by the clinic get a favourable outcome in their case.
Olga Houde, ex-Coordonnatrice Juridique: Olga Houde, former legal coordinator of the Solutions Justes clinic. Photo credit: Ismaël Koné
M<sup>me</sup> Houde a eu l’idée de réal: Ms<sup></sup>. Houde came up with the idea for the research after supporting hundreds of people at the clinic. For her too, luck is a determining factor in the experience of legal support.
« Si la personne rencontre les bonnes pe: “If the person meets the right people, a good employer, caring members of their community, things can go well, but if they cross paths with people who are poorly informed or dishonest, things can really go wrong.”
Maria en sait quelque chose : « J’ai déj: Maria knows something about that: “I’ve already had the experience of paying a lawyer who didn’t do his job. So it’s a dilemma, because you never know when you’ll get a good, professional lawyer and when you won’t.”
À l’écouter, on a l’impression que les i: Listening to her, you get the impression that immigrants have to deal with a kind of lottery: “Some [lawyers] have a true calling to really help people, and others are just there to see how much it represents, I mean, how much money [a client] will represent,” Maria laments.
En fin de compte, elle en a été réduite: In the end, she was reduced to relying on her gut feeling to choose a good representative, “more than on whether they charge you $200 or not,” she says wryly.
<strong>« Votre corps garde une trace qu: “Your body keeps a mark it will never forget”
Cette loterie a, on le comprend, sérieus: As one can understand, this lottery has seriously undermined her well-being, including her mental health. “I think I paid, so to speak. With a lot of physical, mental and emotional health too,” Maria lets out.
Elle évoque, en vrac, des abus au travai: She mentions, in no particular order, abuse at work, physical and psychological abuse by her partner, which she could not report for lack of papers, she specifies. But also accidents that happened during her undeclared work shifts, the legal battle that followed to get compensation and, above all, the contempt she felt the day the judge handed down her verdict. “She’s a woman who makes you understand that your pain doesn’t matter. She throws out a number, as if to say: ‘Get out of here. Go on. Go spend that money with your mother!’”
Toutes ces épreuves, l’avocat ne les ver: The lawyer will see none of these ordeals, she explains: “he won’t know what’s behind his lack of professionalism. Your body keeps a mark it will never forget. You have to pay, and you will pay with your physical health, your emotional health, in your relationships…”
Pour éviter aux immigrants sans statut o: To spare immigrants with no status or precarious status this gauntlet, many community organizations offering legal support services are calling for more substantial government funding.
Selon Camille Bonenfant, organisatrice c: According to Camille Bonenfant, a community organizer in rights advocacy whom we met at the Clinique pour la justice migrante (CJM), the organization regularly turns away immigrants for lack of capacity.
« On est une équipe de huit, mais il y a: “We’re a team of eight, but only three lawyers do legal representation. Right now, migrants with precarious status and no status have an enormous need for legal representation at affordable costs, with legal aid mandates.”
Suivant leur situation, les personnes mi: Depending on their situation, migrants with precarious status or no status do not always have access to legal aid mandates. Not to mention that, “the further along you are in the process, the fewer possibilities there are of finding a lawyer who will take the person on with a legal aid mandate to represent them,” explains Ms<sup></sup>. Bonenfant.
Camille Bonenfant, organisatrice communa: Camille Bonenfant, community organizer in rights advocacy, met at the Clinique pour la justice migrante (CJM). Photo credit: Ismaël Koné
D’après elle, les avocats seraient plus: In her view, lawyers would be more motivated to represent these people if they were better paid by public bodies.
Au-delà des montants alloués, la structu: Beyond the amounts allocated, the structure of the funding affects the supply of services. “The overall mission of the organizations isn’t funded,” says Louis-Philippe Jannard, coordinator of the protection component at the Table de concertation des organismes au service des personnes réfugiées et immigrantes (TCRI). “[That] forces organizations to constantly look for new funding, because projects are often funded for one year, two years, three years, rarely more. So it comes with an enormous administrative burden of searching for funding, but also of accountability reporting.”
Malgré la saturation du système, un bure: Despite the system being overloaded, an immigration legal aid office that had opened in Quebec City in 2023 was closed on April 1<sup>st</sup>, even though demand was, and remains, high.
« Ça plonge les [immigrants] dans l’ince: “That plunges [immigrants] into uncertainty and exposes them to different kinds of abuse and fraud. I’m thinking of people who pass themselves off as lawyers, or of more or less unscrupulous lawyers who will ask for enormous amounts of money for services of truly inadequate quality.”
Pourtant, note Louis-Philippe Jannard, u: Yet, Louis-Philippe Jannard notes, poor legal representation at the start of a migration journey, or ill-advised counsel, has significant consequences later on. “For example, take a person who claims asylum and is poorly advised. Because they’re poorly represented, their claim will be rejected. They have to appeal, have to go before the Federal Court to ask for a judicial review. Those are additional steps that require even more complex legal services.”
<strong>« Comme dans plusieurs autres do: “As in many other areas, we don’t act preventively, we prefer to wait”
Les modifications apportées aux règles d: Changes to immigration rules and new bills also have a major impact on migrants seeking to regularize their situation. These changes are also a major challenge for the workers who support them.
« Par exemple, à l’automne, il y a eu de: “For example, in the fall, there were changes regarding access to permanent residence for people with a temporary work permit. We see it at the Clinique pour la justice migrante: we get more calls, more people contacting us and saying, ‘Oh, but I had a work permit, I lost it; what do I do, how can I stay here?’” explains Camille Bonenfant.
Pour les chercheuses, la volonté politiq: For the researchers, political will is lacking. Yet the country has recorded a marked increase in temporary migration in recent years, particularly in Quebec, where <l1>about 600,000 non-permanent residents live, compared with about 420,000 a year earlier</l1>.
« On est encore dans la logique où on di: “We’re still in the logic of saying that these are people who are here temporarily, who aren’t here to stay. But the reality on the ground is completely different. The Canadian government itself (...) tells us that the vast majority of people who now have permanent residence are people who previously had temporary status,” explains Delphine Nakache.
<l1>Le gouvernement fédéral avait annonc: <l1>The federal government had announced, notably in 2024, a program to regularize immigrants without status</l1>, but then abandoned the idea. According to Ms<sup></sup>. Bonenfant, “that avenue would have benefited thousands of people in Canada who are already here, who work, who have their families here.”
Mais la province prévoit certaines coupe: But the province is planning certain cuts and a freeze on permanent immigration programs for people who are already in the territory. “[Quebec’s] immigration targets are really very low. The suggested scenarios are 25,000, 35,000, 45,000 people a year,” says Mr. Jannard.
Ne pas aider les personnes déjà présente: Not helping the people who are already here amounts, in Delphine Nakache’s view, to creating more precarity and irregularity. “And for the people who, after years, manage to regularize their status, but with enormous difficulty, we create frustration and dissatisfaction.”
Une profonde contrariété sur laquelle tr: It is a deep-seated resentment that Maria has been working on, with the help of therapists, for four years. “If you had met me six months ago, I couldn’t have told you my story,” she says. She now thinks about the next immigrants, and about the people they will meet along the way. “I’d like to raise awareness among professionals in institutions and non-profit organizations so they see that they have people in front of them, and not just numbers,” she concludes.
